title: Full-stack web roadmap
tagline: From a blank machine to a live app in six pages, with free Vietnamese videos.
intro: A path for complete beginners: six pages, one per part, read in order. Every video is free on YouTube and in Vietnamese, with F8 first.
This page is the map. Each page after it goes step by step, from setup to project, with tools current as of 11 October 2026.

sections.title: Six parts
sections.summary: About 150 hours of video, and six months at two hours a day.

blocks.caption: Take them in order: each part builds on everything before it.

items.label: 1. Environment & tools
items.detail: Install a terminal, VS Code, Node.js and Git; learn how the web works
explain: Windows uses WSL to run Ubuntu inside the machine; macOS uses its own Terminal. From then on every command in the path is the same on both.
Node.js goes in through nvm, so switching versions is one command. On 11 October 2026 the LTS release is Node 24.
Git keeps the history of your code and GitHub keeps a copy online. Your first repo is pushed in this very part.

items.label: 2. HTML & CSS
items.detail: Build static pages, lay them out with flexbox, fit every screen
explain: HTML is the frame and CSS the dressing. F8's two projects, The Band and Shopee, take you from the first tag to a full shop page.
It ends with a page you build from a design image, published on GitHub Pages so you have a link to share.

items.label: 3. JavaScript
items.detail: Make pages respond: events, the DOM, calling APIs with fetch
explain: The longest and most important part: React and Node are both JavaScript, so every gap here shows up again later.
Three projects of your own: a to-do app, a validated sign-up form, and a weather app calling a real API.

items.label: 4. ReactJS
items.detail: Split the interface into components, hold data in hooks, change pages with a router
explain: Projects start with Vite instead of the video's Create React App. The page maps every place the old video differs from today's React 19.
The main project is F8's TikTok clone, built with Vite, with the config that replaces the video's customize-cra.

items.label: 5. Node, Express & MySQL
items.detail: Write a server, store data in MySQL, split code into MVC
explain: Express 5 answers requests by route; MySQL keeps the data. It covers installing MySQL on Windows (WSL) and macOS, and joining them with mysql2.
F8's Node video uses Express 4 and older libraries; a table shows each line to change so it runs on current versions.

items.label: 6. Full-stack & deploy
items.detail: A REST API, JWT sign-in, React on top, then online for free
explain: The backend returns JSON, React calls it, and sign-in uses bcrypt and JWT. This is the project for your CV.
Free deployment: MySQL on Aiven, the backend on Render, the frontend on Vercel, step by step with each free plan's limits.

body: Times assume two hours a day, with an hour of your own coding for every hour of video. Going slower is fine; skipping the coding is not.

sections.title: How to study
sections.summary: The videos are half of it; the other half is typing it yourself.

items: Watch one lesson, close the video, and retype the code from memory before moving on.
At the end of each part, build the checklist project with no video open. When stuck, read MDN or react.dev before rewatching.
Commit and push to GitHub after every session, even when the code is unfinished.
Keep a fixed schedule, say two hours a day. Steady beats cramming at the weekend.
Stuck for more than 30 minutes? Ask: say what you are doing, paste the exact error, and list what you tried.
Watching a whole course before coding: by then most of it is forgotten.
Moving to React with shaky JavaScript: every React bug after that is really a JavaScript bug.
Copying code from the video without understanding it: change one detail and you cannot fix it.
Taking several courses on one topic at once: pick one, finish it, then look elsewhere.

sections.title: Using AI while learning
sections.summary: AI helps you understand faster, but it cannot do the typing for you.

items: Paste the error and the code around it, and ask why it fails. Ask for the reason, not just the fixed code.
Ask for a concept explained with a different example from the video, such as closures through a counter.
Write the checklist projects yourself. Letting AI write them skips exactly the part that makes you better.
Check answers against the official docs: MDN, react.dev, expressjs.com. AI may answer for an older version.
Turn off automatic code suggestions in VS Code until the end of part 3, so your hands learn the syntax.

sections.title: Portfolio & job hunting
sections.summary: Employers look at what you built, not at the courses you took.

items: Three projects with live links: a landing page, a React app, a full-stack app
Every repo has a README: a screenshot, features, stack, how to run it
At least one project of your own idea, not a clone from a video
A one-page CV: skills, the three projects with links, and your GitHub
